solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Citizen, bound to be heard, large landowner

parts.note: a national is a citizen of a country

indicators.note: what is heard is a sound, so we want a word that sounds like 'bound'

explanation.surface: A description of a landed citizen who is duty-bound to be listened to.
explanation.walkthrough: The National Trust is a British conservation charity that owns vast stretches of countryside and many stately homes, making it one of the country's largest landowners.
explanation.definitionFit: The National Trust owns more land than almost anyone else in Britain.

clue.text: Lacking staff an advantage at times

parts.note: a wand is a rod or staff

explanation.surface: An understaffed business finding that its short-handedness sometimes helps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' reads as employees, but here it is a stick: NO WAND is being without a staff.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym phrase: something that happens occasionally, not all the time, happens at times.

clue.text: Point about author raised over time

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means the letters are read upwards, so reversed
about means the abbreviation for point goes round the author's word

parts.note: the author of a clue may refer to themselves as ME
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A writer gets promoted, overtaking a stage in their career.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter calls themselves ME. 'Raised' reverses only the point-round-author piece; the over is a cricket term, a set of six balls bowled.
explanation.definitionFit: In music, tempo and time both mean the speed or pace at which a piece is played.

clue.text: Big Oil and BAT playing essential parts

indicators.note: the letters are played with, rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder; BAT is British American Tobacco

explanation.surface: The oil majors and a big tobacco firm playing essential roles in the economy.
explanation.walkthrough: An obbligato is a musical accompaniment that must not be left out; the Italian plural is obbligati. 'Playing' looks like corporate play but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Obbligati are instrumental parts a composer marks as indispensable, so essential parts.

clue.text: God elevated Dail member and writer in style

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting a word up reverses it

parts.note: a TD (Teachta Dála) is a member of the Dáil, the Irish parliament

explanation.surface: A god, an Irish politician and a novelist sharing a sense of style.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dáil is the lower house of the Irish parliament and its members are TDs.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a named design movement of the 1920s and 1930s is one particular style among many.

clue.text: Bone set in hospital usually

indicators.note: the answer is set inside the following words

explanation.surface: A broken bone is normally set in hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'set' a medical verb, but it is telling you the bone is set into the next two words. The talus is the ankle bone.
explanation.definitionFit: The talus is the bone at the top of the foot that forms the ankle joint.

clue.text: Bore in one Parisian river

parts.note: the Derwent, a river in England

explanation.surface: Somebody tedious on the banks of a Paris river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bore' looks like a dull person but is the past tense of bear, as in bore the pain. The Derwent is one of several English rivers of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: To have borne something is to have undergone it: bore = underwent.

clue.text: Prominent feature from Left?

definitions.meaning: reads as a striking characteristic; it is a feature of the landscape that stands up high
reads as a political origin; it is the start of the stock phrase 'from left to right', which wants its missing half

explanation.surface: A striking characteristic that originated on the political left.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'from Left' is half a phrase: its partner, TO R(ight), is the answer. A tor is a rocky hilltop, common on Dartmoor in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A rocky peak rising above moorland is a prominent landscape feature, and it is also what follows 'from L'.

clue.text: Periodically saw firms float

indicators.note: take letters at regular periods, every other one

explanation.surface: Occasionally one sees companies go public.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about business: to float a firm is to sell its shares on the stock market.
explanation.definitionFit: To float in water is to swim, or at least to stay up in it.

clue.text: Struggled rather to concede first lost game

indicators.note: 'first' cuts a letter off

parts.note: MORE is what 'rather to concede' stands for

explanation.surface: A player struggled and preferred to concede the opening game, which was lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lost game' reads as a defeat, but it is a game nobody plays any more: battledore and shuttlecock was the forerunner of badminton. 'Rather' means more, as in more willing.
explanation.definitionFit: Battledore is an old racket game, a lost game in the sense of forgotten.

clue.text: Pub-o'clock, getting round in very quickly

indicators.note: 'getting in' a round is taking it inside, as when you get a round of drinks in
'in' places the round inside the pub-and-time pair, between the two

explanation.surface: When it's time for the pub, someone gets a round in fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pub o'clock' is jokey slang for the hour to start drinking, and 'round' pretends to be a round of drinks; it is only the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: In no time means almost instantly, very quickly.

clue.text: Street artist needing iron to make raking fire

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: A graffiti artist who needs a hot iron to get a fire going.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a street artist stoking a fire; the words are simply three abbreviations in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: To strafe is to attack with sweeping machine-gun fire, typically from low-flying aircraft.

clue.text: Cut the French introduced to suit Goethe's heroine

indicators.note: one word is put inside another

parts.note: Mignon is the girl in Goethe's novel Wilhelm Meister

explanation.surface: A French tailor's cut introduced to dress a Goethe heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' and 'suit' both suggest tailoring, but the cut is of beef.
explanation.definitionFit: Filet mignon is a prized cut of beef from the tenderloin.

clue.text: Bear devouring unruly lad as punishment

indicators.note: one word eats another, holding it inside

parts.note: to harbour, as in harbour a grudge, is to bear it

indicators.note: the letters misbehave, rearranged

explanation.surface: A bear eating an unruly boy as punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' is not the animal but the verb: to harbour, bear or hold.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard labour was a prison sentence of heavy physical work.

clue.text: Ruin beginning to show in desperate couple

indicators.note: the first letter of show goes inside the word for desperate

parts.note: dire means desperate, as in dire need

indicators.note: beginning to means take only the first letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A frantic couple's ruin is beginning to show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruin' reads as a verb in the surface, but it is a noun meaning a decayed state.
explanation.definitionFit: Disrepair is a poor, neglected state of a building, which is ruin in the sense of decay.

clue.text: Kingdom where fruitarians peeled bananas?

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild
peeled removes the outer skin, so the first and last letters go

explanation.surface: A question about where fruit-only eaters would strip their bananas.
explanation.walkthrough: Peeling FRUITARIANS leaves RUITARIAN, which is rearranged. Ruritania is the imaginary kingdom of Anthony Hope's novel The Prisoner of Zenda.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruritania is the fictional Central European realm in The Prisoner of Zenda, a byword for an operetta monarchy.

clue.text: Woman has everyone back on MDMA

indicators.note: in an across clue, X on Y means X comes after Y

parts.note: MDMA is the drug ecstasy, known as E

indicators.note: back means the word for everyone is read in reverse

explanation.surface: A woman shares her ecstasy with the whole party.
explanation.walkthrough: MDMA is the drug ecstasy, known on the street as E.
explanation.definitionFit: Ella is a girl's name, so it can stand for a woman, a common crossword device.

clue.text: Spoils of War?

definitions.note: 'of War?' points to the god of war, so Mars is war personified
definitions.meaning: a verb here: damages or ruins
the Roman god whose domain was war

explanation.surface: The plunder taken in a war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoils of war' is a stock phrase for booty, but 'Spoils' is a verb and 'of War' is the god's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are plain: to mar is to spoil, and the Roman god of war stands for war itself.

clue.text: Not willing to accept Republican way for America

indicators.note: the word takes the letter inside it

explanation.surface: Someone refusing to accept a Republican path for the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not willing' reads as reluctant, but it means without a will: someone who dies intestate leaves none.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the US federal highway network links the states, so it is a road, a way, for America.

clue.text: Flyer soon welcomed by workers' association

indicators.note: taken in by, so it goes inside

explanation.surface: A leaflet shortly to be welcomed by a union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flyer' looks like a leaflet but is a bird: the tinamou is a ground bird of Central and South America.
explanation.definitionFit: A tinamou is a bird, and birds are flyers.

clue.text: Releasing uranium, home visitor's put away

indicators.note: letting go of the letter, so it is removed

parts.note: U is the chemical symbol for uranium, removed from GUEST

explanation.surface: A radioactive house guest being locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put away' is slang for eating a lot, as in he put away three pies.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to put food away is colloquial for eating it, taking it into the body.

clue.text: Retire having abandoned one North European city

indicators.note: to abandon something is to leave it behind

parts.note: to turn in is to go to bed, to retire
N = North; one of the two Ns is dropped

explanation.surface: Someone retiring and leaving a northern European city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'North European' looks like one phrase, but 'one North' goes with the deletion and the city is simply European.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the answer is one city in Europe, the Piedmont capital in northern Italy.

clue.text: NZ Rail in evil nonsense about going westward

indicators.note: in an across clue, going west means reading right to left

explanation.surface: Bad nonsense about a railway line in New Zealand heading west.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rail' looks like a railway, but it is the bird family: the notornis, or takahe, is a flightless rail from New Zealand.
explanation.definitionFit: Notornis is the genus of the takahe, a New Zealand rail.

clue.text: Sage from Dublin bringing down leader?

indicators.note: in a down clue, the first letter moves to the bottom

parts.note: someone from Dublin is Irish; I moves from the top to the bottom

explanation.surface: A wise person from Dublin who topples a leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bringing down leader' suggests a coup, and the question mark nods to Rishi Sunak, a British prime minister; here it only moves the I to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A borrowing from Sanskrit: in Hindu tradition an inspired poet-seer goes by this title, so it names a sage.

clue.text: Trooper left ragtag army in Irish county

indicators.note: the letters for 'left ragtag army' are placed inside the county's name

parts.note: Cavan is a county in Ireland

indicators.note: ragtag means disorderly, so the letters of army are jumbled

explanation.surface: A soldier abandoned a scruffy army somewhere in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: Cavan is a county in the Republic of Ireland. 'Left' is not a verb meaning departed; it is the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A trooper is a soldier in a cavalry regiment, a mounted soldier.

clue.text: Commercials Saudis used at regular intervals

indicators.note: letters taken at a fixed, repeating spacing, here every second one

explanation.surface: Saudi Arabia running television adverts regularly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Used' only joins: the Saudis' letters are used at regular intervals.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, shortened: adverts on TV or radio are commercials.

clue.text: Degenerate son with tattoos

explanation.surface: A dissolute son covered in tattoos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Degenerate' looks like an adjective or noun describing the son, but it is the verb: to degenerate is to sink.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as verbs: to degenerate is to decline morally, to go downhill.

clue.text: Restrictive practice a signal to turn nasty

indicators.note: the letters take a bad turn

explanation.surface: A restrictive work rule that is a warning sign things are about to get ugly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Restrictive practice' is a trade-union term for rules limiting output; here it is taken literally, as squeezing a throat.
explanation.definitionFit: Strangulation restricts the airway, a restrictive practice in the literal sense.
